subtopics.name: Statement and form
points: Every particle attracts every other with a force along the line joining them
F = G m1 m2 / r^2, where G = 6.674 x 10^-11 N m^2 kg^-2
The force is always attractive and acts on both bodies equally (Newton's third law)

subtopics.name: Why G matters
points: G is a universal constant, the same everywhere and for all masses
It is extremely small, which is why gravity is negligible between everyday objects
Cavendish first measured G in 1798 using a torsion balance

subtopics.name: Inverse square behaviour
points: Doubling the separation reduces the force to one quarter
The law is an inverse square because the force spreads over a spherical surface of area 4 pi r^2
Valid for point masses and for uniform spheres treated as point masses at their centres

subtopics.name: Superposition
points: The net force on a mass is the vector sum of forces from all other masses
Forces from different bodies add independently
This is what makes n-body problems hard but tractable

branches.topic: Level 3 — Upgraded: limits and modern view

subtopics.name: Where the law breaks down
points: Fails at very strong fields and high speeds — general relativity is required
Anomalous perihelion precession of Mercury was the first observed failure
Gravitational waves and black holes have no Newtonian description

subtopics.name: Field formulation
points: Gravity can be described as a field g = GM/r^2 rather than as action at a distance
Field lines point toward the mass and never cross
Field formulation is what generalises to relativity

subtopics.name: The inverse square law
points: F = G m1 m2 / r^2
Proportional to both masses, inversely proportional to the square of separation
Direction along the line joining the centres

subtopics.name: Deriving g
points: Weight = mg and weight = GMm/R^2, so g = GM/R^2
g depends only on the planet's mass and radius, not on the falling body
Explains why all bodies fall at the same rate in vacuum

subtopics.name: Kepler connection
points: Newton showed Kepler's laws follow from the inverse square law
T^2 proportional to r^3 for circular orbits
Gives a way to measure planetary masses from orbital data

subtopics.name: Measurement of G
points: Cavendish torsion balance measured the tiny attraction between lead spheres
Knowing G lets us weigh the Earth
Modern value 6.67430 x 10^-11, with the weakest precision of any fundamental constant

class-11/physics/gravitation/variation-i.centralConcept: How g changes with height and depth

subtopics.name: At the surface
points: g = GM/R^2, about 9.8 m/s^2 on Earth
R is the Earth's radius, about 6400 km
g is maximum at the surface, not at the centre

subtopics.name: Altitude
points: g_h = g (1 - 2h/R) for h much smaller than R
Exact form: g_h = GM/(R+h)^2
g decreases with height, falling to zero at infinity

subtopics.name: Depth
points: g_d = g (1 - d/R) for depth d
g decreases linearly with depth inside a uniform Earth
At the centre g = 0 because the mass pulls equally in all directions

subtopics.name: Altitude versus depth
points: For the same small distance, the decrease with depth is twice the decrease with altitude
Reason: at depth only the inner sphere attracts; at altitude the whole mass attracts from farther away
g falls off as 1/r^2 outside but linearly inside

subtopics.name: Other variations
points: g is less at the equator than the poles because of rotation and equatorial bulge
g decreases slightly with latitude-independent factors such as local rock density
Rotation contributes a centrifugal term that reduces apparent g at the equator

class-11/physics/gravitation/variation-g.centralConcept: Variation of g with altitude and depth

subtopics.name: Base relation
points: g = GM/R^2 at the surface
Any change in effective distance or enclosed mass changes g
Altitude changes distance; depth changes enclosed mass

subtopics.name: Formulas
points: g_h = g(1 - 2h/R) for small h
g_d = g(1 - d/R)
Equating them gives the classic result that the decrease at depth d equals the decrease at altitude 2d

subtopics.name: Exam application
points: A common question asks at what depth g falls to half its surface value — answer d = R/2
Another asks where g is the same at altitude and depth — answer h = d/2
Always state whether the Earth is assumed uniform

class-11/physics/gravitation/escape-velo.centralConcept: Escape velocity — the speed to break free

subtopics.name: Definition
points: The minimum speed needed to escape a gravitational field without further propulsion
Derived by setting total mechanical energy to zero at infinity
Independent of the direction of projection and of the projectile's mass

subtopics.name: Derivation and value
points: Kinetic energy at surface equals magnitude of potential energy: 1/2 m v^2 = GMm/R
v_e = sqrt(2GM/R) = sqrt(2gR)
For Earth: about 11.2 km/s

subtopics.name: Scaling
points: v_e is proportional to sqrt(M/R)
Moon's escape velocity is about 2.4 km/s because of its small mass
Escape velocity from a black hole's event horizon exceeds the speed of light

subtopics.name: Orbital versus escape
points: Orbital velocity v_o = sqrt(GM/r) at radius r
v_e = sqrt(2) x v_o — escape is always 1.414 times orbital speed
This ratio holds for any body and any circular orbit

subtopics.name: Atmospheric and practical limits
points: Escape velocity is a lower bound; atmospheric drag and Earth's rotation modify the practical requirement
Launching eastward from the equator gains about 460 m/s from rotation
Gas molecules escape a planet's atmosphere when their thermal speed approaches v_e

class-11/physics/gravitation/motion-of-a.centralConcept: Satellite motion — orbital velocity and period

subtopics.name: Why a satellite stays up
points: Gravity provides exactly the centripetal force needed for circular motion
A satellite is in continuous free fall, but its tangential speed keeps it missing the Earth
No propulsion is needed once in a stable orbit

branches.topic: Level 2 — Core: the two key formulas

subtopics.name: Orbital velocity
points: GMm/r^2 = mv^2/r gives v = sqrt(GM/r)
v decreases as orbital radius increases
For a low Earth orbit v is about 7.9 km/s

subtopics.name: Time period
points: T = 2 pi r / v = 2 pi sqrt(r^3/GM)
T^2 proportional to r^3 — this is Kepler's third law
Higher orbits are slower and take longer

branches.topic: Level 3 — Upgraded: energy and special orbits

subtopics.name: Energy of a satellite
points: KE = GMm/2r, PE = -GMm/r, total E = -GMm/2r
Total energy is negative for a bound orbit
Total energy equals half the potential energy — a standard exam result

subtopics.name: Geostationary orbit
points: Period exactly 24 hours, equatorial, prograde, giving a fixed point above the ground
Radius about 42,000 km from the Earth's centre, altitude about 36,000 km
Used for communication and weather satellites

subtopics.name: The centripetal condition
points: Gravitational force equals the required centripetal force
This single condition yields both orbital speed and period
Assumes a circular orbit; elliptical orbits need Kepler's laws

subtopics.name: Key results
points: v = sqrt(GM/r), T = 2 pi sqrt(r^3/GM)
v_e = sqrt(2) v_o
Total energy = -GMm/2r

subtopics.name: Weightlessness
points: Astronauts in orbit are not free of gravity — they are in free fall
Apparent weightlessness arises because everything falls together
g at the ISS altitude is still about 8.7 m/s^2

subtopics.name: Orbit types
points: Low Earth orbit (200-2000 km) for observation and the ISS
Geostationary (36,000 km) for communication
Polar and sun-synchronous orbits for imaging and remote sensing

class-11/physics/gravitation/geostationa.centralConcept: Geostationary satellite — a fixed point in the sky

subtopics.name: Three requirements
points: Period must equal one sidereal day, about 23 h 56 min
Orbit must be equatorial, otherwise the satellite drifts north and south
Orbit must be prograde, moving in the same sense as Earth's rotation

subtopics.name: Radius and altitude
points: From T = 2 pi sqrt(r^3/GM) with T = 86400 s, r is about 4.22 x 10^7 m
Altitude above the surface is about 36,000 km
Orbital speed is about 3.07 km/s

subtopics.name: Uses
points: Communication and broadcasting — a fixed antenna can point permanently
Weather monitoring of a full hemisphere continuously
Three satellites 120 degrees apart cover most of the globe

subtopics.name: Geostationary versus geosynchronous
points: Geosynchronous means matching the rotation period; the orbit may be inclined
Geostationary is a special case that is also equatorial and circular
An inclined geosynchronous satellite traces a figure-of-eight in the sky

subtopics.name: Limitations
points: High altitude means a long signal delay of about 0.24 s round trip
Poor coverage of polar regions
Slots in the equatorial belt are a finite and contested resource

subtopics.name: Definition
points: Field strength g is the force per unit mass experienced by a small test mass
g = F/m = GM/r^2
It is a vector, directed toward the attracting mass

subtopics.name: Field lines
points: Lines point toward the mass; closer lines mean a stronger field
Lines never cross, because the field has one direction at each point
Uniform field is represented by parallel equally spaced lines

subtopics.name: Field versus acceleration
points: Numerically g equals the acceleration of a freely falling body
This equivalence is the weak equivalence principle
Units are N/kg or m/s^2, dimensionally identical

subtopics.name: Inside and outside a shell
points: Outside a uniform spherical shell, the field is as if all mass were at the centre
Inside a uniform shell the field is exactly zero
This is Newton's shell theorem and it underpins the depth formula for g

subtopics.name: Potential energy
points: U = -GMm/r, with zero defined at infinity
Negative because gravity is attractive and work must be done to separate the masses
Near the surface this reduces to U = mgh

subtopics.name: Potential
points: V = U/m = -GM/r, the work per unit mass to bring a unit mass from infinity
Potential is a scalar, so it adds algebraically with no vector work
Units are J/kg

subtopics.name: Relation to field
points: g = -dV/dr — field strength is the negative potential gradient
Potential decreases toward the mass; field points in the direction of decreasing potential
Equipotential surfaces are perpendicular to field lines

subtopics.name: Work done
points: Work done moving a mass between two points equals m times the potential difference
Work done along an equipotential is zero
Work done depends only on endpoints, not the path — gravity is conservative

subtopics.name: Escape and binding
points: Total energy zero means the body just escapes
Binding energy is the energy needed to remove a mass to infinity
For a satellite, total energy is -GMm/2r and binding energy is +GMm/2r

subtopics.name: Standard traps
points: Potential at the centre of a uniform sphere is finite, not infinite
Potential inside a shell is constant and equals its surface value
Do not confuse potential (J/kg) with potential energy (J)

class-11/physics/gravitation/centre-of-m.centralConcept: Centre of mass and centre of gravity

subtopics.name: Centre of mass
points: The point where the entire mass of a system may be considered concentrated for translational motion
For two masses, it divides the separation in inverse ratio to the masses
It is a property of the mass distribution alone

subtopics.name: Centre of gravity
points: The point where the total gravitational force may be considered to act
Coincides with the centre of mass in a uniform gravitational field
Differs from it only over distances where g varies appreciably

subtopics.name: Formulas
points: For a uniform body the centre of mass is at its geometric centre
For a hollow shape it may lie outside the material

subtopics.name: Stability
points: A body topples when its centre of gravity falls outside its base
Lower centre of gravity and wider base mean greater stability
Explains why racing cars are built low and wide

subtopics.name: Motion of the centre of mass
points: The centre of mass moves as if all external forces acted on all the mass there
Internal forces cannot change the motion of the centre of mass
Explains why a exploding shell's fragments have a centre of mass continuing on the original parabola

subtopics.name: Current
points: Current is the rate of flow of charge: I = Q/t
Conventional current flows opposite to electron flow
Unit ampere; 1 A = 1 C/s

subtopics.name: Drift velocity
points: Electrons drift slowly in the direction opposite the field, superimposed on random thermal motion
Typical drift speed is about 10^-4 m/s, far slower than the signal speed
The electric field propagates at nearly the speed of light, which is why a lamp lights instantly

subtopics.name: I = nAev_d
points: n is free electron density, A cross-sectional area, e electronic charge, v_d drift velocity
Current depends on drift velocity, not on the random thermal speed
Larger area or higher electron density gives more current for the same drift speed

subtopics.name: Why drift is slow
points: Electrons collide constantly with the lattice and lose directed momentum
The drift velocity is the small average velocity superimposed on thermal motion
Increasing temperature increases collisions and reduces drift velocity, raising resistivity

subtopics.name: Current density and mobility
points: J = I/A = n e v_d, a vector quantity
Mobility mu = v_d/E measures how easily carriers move
Conductivity sigma = n e mu

subtopics.name: Numerical anchors
points: For copper, n is about 8.5 x 10^28 per cubic metre
A 1 A current in a 1 mm^2 wire gives drift velocity of order 10^-4 m/s
Electron thermal speed at room temperature is about 10^5 m/s

subtopics.name: The law
points: V = IR at constant temperature
Resistance is the opposition to current flow, measured in ohms
Ohm's law is empirical, not a fundamental law of nature

subtopics.name: Resistivity
points: R = rho L / A, where rho is resistivity, a material property
Resistivity depends on material and temperature, not on shape
Resistance depends on both material and geometry

subtopics.name: Temperature dependence
points: For metals, rho increases with temperature: rho = rho_0 (1 + alpha dT)
For semiconductors, resistivity DECREASES with temperature as more carriers are freed
This opposite behaviour distinguishes metals from semiconductors

subtopics.name: Ohmic versus non-ohmic
points: Ohmic conductors give a straight V-I line through the origin
Non-ohmic devices (diodes, filament lamps, thermistors) give curved or asymmetric graphs
A filament lamp's resistance rises as it heats

subtopics.name: Microscopic origin
points: Drude model: electrons accelerate in the field and lose momentum in collisions
R = rho L/A follows from I = nAev_d and v_d = eE tau/m
Explains why longer, thinner wires have more resistance

subtopics.name: Superconductivity
points: Below a critical temperature some materials drop to zero resistance
Persistent currents flow without energy loss
Used in MRI magnets and maglev systems

class-11/physics/dc-circuits/resistances.centralConcept: Series and parallel combinations of resistors

subtopics.name: Series
points: Same current through every resistor
Total voltage divides among them
R_eq = R1 + R2 + R3

subtopics.name: Parallel
points: Same voltage across every resistor
Total current divides among them

subtopics.name: Behaviour of the equivalent resistance
points: Series equivalent is always larger than the largest individual resistance
Parallel equivalent is always smaller than the smallest individual resistance
Two equal resistors in parallel give half the value

subtopics.name: Power and division
points: Series: larger resistance dissipates more power (P = I^2 R)
Parallel: smaller resistance dissipates more power (P = V^2/R)
Potential divider: V1 = V x R1/(R1+R2)

subtopics.name: Why houses use parallel
points: Parallel connection gives each appliance the full supply voltage
Each device can be switched independently
A failure in one branch does not break the others

subtopics.name: Symmetry shortcuts
points: A balanced Wheatstone bridge has no current through the galvanometer
Infinite resistor chains and cube networks reduce by symmetry
Always redraw before calculating — most errors are drawing errors

subtopics.name: Definitions
points: EMF is the total energy per unit charge supplied by the source
Terminal potential difference is the voltage actually available to the external circuit
Internal resistance r is the resistance within the source itself

subtopics.name: The key relation
points: V = E - Ir, where E is EMF and r internal resistance
Terminal voltage falls as current rises
When no current flows, terminal voltage equals EMF

subtopics.name: Power
points: Total power E I splits into I^2 R (external) and I^2 r (internal loss)
Maximum power transfer to the load occurs when R = r
At maximum power transfer the efficiency is only 50%

subtopics.name: Cells in series
points: EMFs add; internal resistances add
Useful when a higher voltage is needed
One reversed cell subtracts its EMF

subtopics.name: Cells in parallel
points: EMF stays the same; internal resistance falls
Useful when a higher current is needed
Only identical cells should be paralleled, or circulating currents arise

subtopics.name: Work done
points: Work done moving charge Q through potential difference V is W = QV
Since Q = It, W = VIt
Unit joule

subtopics.name: Power
points: P = W/t = VI
Using Ohm's law: P = I^2 R = V^2/R
Unit watt; commercial unit is the kilowatt-hour

subtopics.name: Choosing the right form
points: Use P = I^2 R when current is common (series)
Use P = V^2/R when voltage is common (parallel)
All three forms are equivalent only for an ohmic resistor

subtopics.name: Heating effect
points: Joule heating: H = I^2 R t
This is the basis of electric heaters, fuses and filament lamps
It is also the source of transmission loss

subtopics.name: Why power is transmitted at high voltage
points: Loss in cables is I^2 R, so reducing current cuts loss quadratically
Stepping up voltage reduces current for the same power
This is why national grids use high-voltage AC transmission

subtopics.name: Units and billing
points: Domestic billing is in units of kWh
A 100 W bulb left on for 10 hours uses 1 unit

subtopics.name: First law — inertia
points: A body remains at rest or in uniform motion unless acted on by a net external force
Defines force as the cause of change in motion
Inertia is the resistance to change in motion, measured by mass

subtopics.name: Second law — F = ma
points: Net force equals rate of change of momentum: F = dp/dt
For constant mass this reduces to F = ma
Force and acceleration are both vectors, in the same direction

subtopics.name: Third law — action-reaction
points: Every action has an equal and opposite reaction
The pair acts on DIFFERENT bodies, which is why they do not cancel
Explains walking, rocket propulsion and recoil

subtopics.name: Free body diagrams
points: Draw every force acting ON the body, never forces it exerts
Choose axes along the likely acceleration
Resolve forces and apply F = ma along each axis

subtopics.name: Common force types
points: Weight mg downward, normal reaction perpendicular to the surface
Tension along the string, friction opposing relative motion
Spring force proportional to extension

subtopics.name: Inertial and non-inertial frames
points: Newton's laws hold only in inertial (non-accelerating) frames
In an accelerating frame a pseudo force -ma must be added
Centrifugal force is a pseudo force of this kind

subtopics.name: Limits of validity
points: Fails at speeds near c — special relativity is required
Fails at atomic scales — quantum mechanics is required
Within its domain it is exact, which is why engineering still uses it

subtopics.name: Momentum
points: p = mv, a vector in the direction of velocity
Unit kg m/s
Newton's second law in its general form is F = dp/dt

subtopics.name: Impulse
points: Impulse = F x t = change in momentum
Area under a force-time graph gives impulse
Explains why airbags and crumple zones reduce injury — longer time, smaller force

subtopics.name: Law of conservation of momentum
points: Total momentum of an isolated system stays constant
Follows from Newton's third law — internal forces cancel in pairs
Applies to all collisions and explosions

subtopics.name: Collisions
points: Elastic: momentum and kinetic energy both conserved
Inelastic: momentum conserved, kinetic energy lost to heat and deformation
Perfectly inelastic: bodies stick together and move with common velocity

subtopics.name: Coefficient of restitution
points: e = relative velocity of separation / relative velocity of approach
e = 1 for elastic, e = 0 for perfectly inelastic
Energy loss relates directly to e

subtopics.name: Centre of mass view
points: In a collision the centre of mass continues unaffected by internal forces
Working in the centre-of-mass frame simplifies collision problems
Explains why total momentum is conserved even when energy is not

subtopics.name: Moment of a force
points: Torque = force x perpendicular distance from the pivot
Unit newton metre
Torque is a vector, given by the cross product of r and F

subtopics.name: Couple
points: Two equal, opposite, parallel forces with different lines of action
Produces pure rotation with no net translational force
Torque of a couple = force x perpendicular separation

subtopics.name: Conditions for equilibrium
points: Net force must be zero (translational equilibrium)
Net torque about any point must be zero (rotational equilibrium)
Both conditions are required for complete equilibrium

subtopics.name: Principle of moments
points: Sum of clockwise moments equals sum of anticlockwise moments
Used to solve lever, beam and balance problems
Choose the pivot to eliminate an unknown force

subtopics.name: Types of equilibrium
points: Stable: displaced slightly, returns — centre of gravity rises
Unstable: displaced slightly, moves further away — centre of gravity falls
Neutral: no tendency to return or move away

subtopics.name: Applications
points: Levers, seesaws and wheelbarrows are moment problems
Ladder problems combine moments with friction
Torque is the rotational analogue of force, with I as the analogue of mass

subtopics.name: Types
points: Static friction acts before motion starts
Kinetic friction acts during sliding
Rolling friction is much smaller than sliding friction

subtopics.name: The laws
points: Friction is proportional to the normal reaction: f = mu N
Friction is independent of the apparent area of contact
Static friction exceeds kinetic friction for the same surfaces

subtopics.name: Angle of friction
points: tan(lambda) = mu, where lambda is the angle of friction
The resultant of normal reaction and limiting friction makes this angle with the normal
Angle of repose equals the angle of friction

subtopics.name: Angle of repose
points: The steepest angle at which a body rests without sliding
tan(theta) = mu_s
Independent of the mass of the body

subtopics.name: Microscopic origin
points: Friction arises from adhesion at real contact points and surface roughness
Real contact area is far smaller than apparent area, which is why area does not matter
Lubrication works by separating surfaces with a fluid film

subtopics.name: Necessary friction
points: Walking, braking, belt drives and nails all depend on friction
Friction is not simply a nuisance to be eliminated
Anti-lock brakes exploit static friction by preventing skidding

subtopics.name: Work
points: W = F d cos(theta), the component of force along displacement
Work is zero when force is perpendicular to displacement
Unit joule; work can be negative when force opposes motion

subtopics.name: The theorem
points: Net work done on a body equals its change in kinetic energy
W_net = KE_final - KE_initial = 1/2 m v^2 - 1/2 m u^2
Holds for all forces, conservative or not

subtopics.name: Work by a variable force
points: W = integral of F dx, the area under a force-displacement graph
For a spring, W = 1/2 k x^2
Graphical area is often the fastest route in exams

subtopics.name: Kinetic energy
points: KE = 1/2 m v^2, always positive
Scales with the square of speed, which is why braking distance quadruples when speed doubles
Momentum and kinetic energy are related by KE = p^2/2m

subtopics.name: Why the theorem is powerful
points: It converts a force problem into an energy accounting problem
Avoids needing the detailed path when only endpoints matter
Especially useful for friction and variable forces

subtopics.name: Limits
points: Requires an inertial frame
Kinetic energy is frame-dependent, so the theorem must be applied in one consistent frame
For rotational motion a rotational analogue exists with moment of inertia

subtopics.name: The principle
points: Total mechanical energy stays constant when only conservative forces act
KE + PE = constant
Energy is transformed, never created or destroyed

subtopics.name: Conservative forces
points: Work done depends only on endpoints, not the path
Gravity and spring force are conservative
A closed loop gives zero net work

subtopics.name: Non-conservative forces
points: Friction and air resistance are non-conservative
Work done by them removes mechanical energy as heat
Modified statement: KE + PE + work by friction = constant

subtopics.name: Potential energy
points: PE is defined only for conservative forces
Gravitational PE = mgh near the surface, -GMm/r in general
Spring PE = 1/2 k x^2

subtopics.name: Energy graphs
points: Plot PE against position; KE is the gap up to total energy
Turning points occur where KE becomes zero
The negative gradient of the PE curve gives the force

subtopics.name: Broader conservation
points: Total energy including heat is always conserved
Mass-energy equivalence extends this to nuclear processes
Perpetual motion machines fail precisely because of this principle

subtopics.name: What is conserved
points: Momentum is conserved in ALL collisions
Kinetic energy is conserved only in elastic collisions
Total energy is always conserved

subtopics.name: Elastic collision
points: Both momentum and kinetic energy conserved
Relative speed of approach equals relative speed of separation
For equal masses in 1D, the bodies exchange velocities

subtopics.name: Perfectly inelastic collision
points: Bodies stick together and move with a common velocity
Maximum kinetic energy loss of any collision type

subtopics.name: Coefficient of restitution
points: e = 1 elastic, e = 0 perfectly inelastic, 0 < e < 1 partially elastic
Fractional energy loss = 1 - e^2

subtopics.name: Frame of reference
points: In the centre-of-mass frame, an elastic collision simply reverses both velocities
This makes elastic collision problems far simpler
Inelastic collisions look asymmetric in the lab frame but symmetric in the CM frame

class-11/physics/nuclear-physics/nucleus.centralConcept: Discovery and structure of the nucleus

subtopics.name: Rutherford's gold foil experiment
points: Alpha particles fired at thin gold foil, 1911
Most passed straight through, some deflected sharply, a few bounced back
Conclusion: positive charge and nearly all mass are concentrated in a tiny central nucleus

subtopics.name: Earlier discoveries
points: Thomson discovered the electron in 1897 (cathode rays)
Goldstein discovered the proton in 1886 (canal rays)
Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932

subtopics.name: Composition and notation
points: Nucleus contains protons (Z) and neutrons (N); mass number A = Z + N
Notation: A over Z before the element symbol
Isotopes have the same Z but different N

subtopics.name: Size and density
points: Nuclear radius R = R0 A^(1/3), with R0 about 1.2 x 10^-15 m
Nuclear density is roughly constant across all nuclei, about 2.3 x 10^17 kg/m^3
The nucleus is about 10^5 times smaller than the atom but holds almost all its mass

subtopics.name: Nuclear forces
points: Strong nuclear force binds nucleons, is short-ranged and charge-independent
It is strongly attractive at about 1-2 fm and repulsive at very short range
Competes with electrostatic repulsion between protons, which limits nucleus size

subtopics.name: Why heavy nuclei are unstable
points: Coulomb repulsion grows as Z^2 while the strong force grows only as A
Beyond bismuth (Z = 83) no stable nucleus exists
Explains alpha decay and spontaneous fission in heavy elements

subtopics.name: The relation
points: E = mc^2, proposed by Einstein in 1905
Mass and energy are two forms of the same quantity
1 kg of mass corresponds to about 9 x 10^16 J

subtopics.name: Practical units
points: 1 u = 931.5 MeV of energy
Electron mass 0.511 MeV/c^2, proton 938.3 MeV/c^2
Using MeV makes nuclear calculations tractable

subtopics.name: Mass defect
points: The mass of a nucleus is less than the sum of its constituent nucleons
Delta m = (Z m_p + N m_n) - M_nucleus
The missing mass appears as binding energy

subtopics.name: Binding energy
points: BE = Delta m x c^2
Binding energy per nucleon measures nuclear stability
Peaks at about 8.8 MeV per nucleon near iron-56

subtopics.name: Why fission and fusion both release energy
points: Fission splits heavy nuclei toward the iron peak, increasing BE per nucleon
Fusion combines light nuclei toward the peak, also increasing BE per nucleon
Both move the system toward maximum stability

subtopics.name: Packing fraction
points: Packing fraction = (M - A)/A, a measure of departure from A units
Negative packing fraction means the nucleus is bound and stable
A curve of packing fraction against mass number reveals the same iron peak

subtopics.name: Fission
points: A heavy nucleus splits into two lighter nuclei plus neutrons
Example: U-235 + n gives Ba-141 + Kr-92 + 3n
Releases about 200 MeV per fission event

subtopics.name: Fusion
points: Two light nuclei combine into a heavier one
Example: four protons fuse to helium in the Sun
Releases more energy per unit mass than fission

subtopics.name: Chain reaction
points: Each fission releases neutrons that can trigger further fissions
Critical mass is the minimum mass needed to sustain the chain
Controlled in a reactor by moderators and control rods

subtopics.name: Fusion conditions
points: Requires extremely high temperature to overcome Coulomb repulsion
Requires high density and sufficient confinement time
Lawson criterion sets the threshold for net energy gain

subtopics.name: Energy comparison
points: Fusion releases about 4 times more energy per kilogram than fission
Fusion fuel (deuterium) is abundant in seawater
Fusion produces far less long-lived radioactive waste

subtopics.name: Practical status
points: Fission is commercially mature and supplies about 10% of world electricity
Fusion remains experimental; ITER is the flagship project
The Sun is the only proven sustained fusion reactor

subtopics.name: Pair production
points: A high-energy photon converts into an electron-positron pair
Requires a nearby nucleus to conserve momentum
Threshold energy is 2 x 0.511 = 1.022 MeV

subtopics.name: Annihilation
points: An electron and positron combine and disappear, producing two photons
Two photons are needed to conserve momentum
Each photon carries 0.511 MeV

subtopics.name: Conservation laws
points: Charge, momentum, angular momentum and total energy are conserved
Mass number and lepton number are conserved
Energy and mass are interconverted via E = mc^2

subtopics.name: Threshold condition
points: Photon energy must be at least 2 m_e c^2
Excess energy becomes kinetic energy of the pair
Cannot occur in empty space without a third body for momentum balance

subtopics.name: Applications
points: PET scans detect the two 511 keV photons from positron annihilation
Annihilation explains why antimatter cannot persist in ordinary matter
Pair production sets an upper limit on gamma-ray propagation across the universe

class-11/physics/nuclear-physics/atomic-.centralConcept: Atomic mass, isotopes and nuclear notation

subtopics.name: Atomic mass unit
points: 1 u is one twelfth the mass of a carbon-12 atom
Atomic masses are measured relative to carbon-12 by definition

subtopics.name: Isotopes
points: Same number of protons, different number of neutrons
Chemically almost identical, physically different in mass and stability
Example: U-235 and U-238

subtopics.name: Average atomic mass
points: Weighted average over natural isotopic abundances
Chlorine's 35.5 arises from 75% Cl-35 and 25% Cl-37
Not an integer because it is an abundance-weighted mean

subtopics.name: Isobars and isotones
points: Isobars: same mass number A, different Z
Isotones: same number of neutrons N
Isomers: same nucleus in different energy states

subtopics.name: Why isotopes matter
points: U-235 is fissile while U-238 is not — enrichment separates them
Carbon-14 dating relies on the fixed ratio of C-14 to C-12 in living things
Medical isotopes such as Tc-99m are chosen for half-life and decay mode
